title: TA9-02039
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX is a 50-year-old female citizen of Guyana, who claims refugee protection pursuant to Sections 96 and 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

In making the assessment in this claim the panel considered the claimant's oral and written testimony and submissions, documentary evidence entered, before and at the hearing, which included counsel's submissions post hearing.2

The issues that were identified at the outset were: Exclusion, 1 F(b); identity; credibility; subjective fear, such as delay in claiming, and failure to claim elsewhere, due to a period of residence in the United States of America (USA) and state protection.

The issue of Exclusion had been raised by the Minister,3 pursuant to Rule 25.4 The claimant was detained on XXXX XXXX, 20095 upon arriving at Pearson Airport. She made her claim that day.6 The claimant filed her Personal Information Form (PIF) on February 25, 2009,7 an amendment on May 24, 2011.8 The Minister provided a Notice of Intent to Intervene on February 17 and 18, 2010.9 Allegations

The claimant alleges that she fears returning to Guyana because she was the victim of domestic abuse by XXXX XXXX, a man whom she moved in with from 1980 to 1987, XXXX, Guyana. XXXX XXXX told the claimant, who was at that time known as XXXX XXXX, he was a XXXX, and would threaten the claimant with a handgun, if she did not do what he wanted her to do. The claimant went to the police on several occasions for their help, but they did not help her because they were friends with XXXX, her tormentor. In 1987, she ran away to stay at another friends' home in XXXX. While there, she met a man called Horriss who, after learning about her troubles, offered to get her out of Guyana, by sponsoring her in a marriage to him in the USA. In 1988, she married XXXX, and took his last name, XXXX. By XXXX 1989, she traveled to the USA and entered the country as a permanent resident10. By this time, she was pregnant with the child of another man she had been dating called XXXX XXXX. Since she had no medical insurance in the USA, she returned to Guyana, to have her baby born there, between XXXX and XXXX 1989. She left the child in the care of her mother, the woman who had raised her, XXXX XXXX. Despite having had another boyfriend, XXXX, adopted her son, who was an older child, from an earlier man.
In 1991, the claimant had been charged, with grand larceny, and was convicted in the spring of 1992, due to a matter involving fraudulent credits on credit cards, while working at XXXX.

The claimant returned to Guyana in early 1992, to see both of her children. While there, she got pregnant with a third child, from the man she had been dating called XXXX XXXX. The third child was born in XXXX XXXX XXXX 1992, in Guyana. In XXXX 1992, XXXX tragically died in a car accident, in Guyana, and the claimant returned to the USA.
In 1993, the claimant saw XXXX XXXX at a Guyanese restaurant in New York, while with two of her children. She believes he was in the US due his connections from being XXXX XXXX XXXX.

The claimant returned to Guyana, to attend a funeral of one of XXXX sons. While at the funeral, she saw XXXX, who forced her to go to his house, by using a gun. She stayed with him, despite his crazed behavior for a few days, and left to go to Essiquibo where she stayed for two weeks. She returned to the USA, after returning to XXXX for a day.
After returning the claimant learned that her children had been taken by XXXX, after she left, as XXXX told XXXX, that she had given him authority to take them.

In 1995, the claimant was charged with forgery while working as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. She was sentenced to 1-3 years in jail, and was supposed to serve 6 months in a boot camp, but due to medical issues, she did not. She completed her sentence.
In 1999, the claimant returned to Guyana. The claimant remained in Guayana, in hiding, living in various places sometimes with friends and other times, with XXXX, by force.

In XXXX 2004, she obtained travel documents still under the name XXXX XXXX, and departed Guyana, to go to the USA, through Mexico. The claimant obtained a job, and stayed in Brooklyn. XXXX, found her in the USA, and took her back with him, again by force, where he was violent towards her. She escaped and went to Port Washington, Long Island, where she found work, in 2005. She was able to find another job, by assuming the identity of XXXX XXXX, her cousin.

In 2006, the claimant was arrested, and charged with falsification of documents, and she was incarcerated until XXXX 2008. At this time she lost her Permanent Resident Status in the USA, and on XXXX XXXX, 2008, she was deported to Guyana. As a result of the deportation, she was detained on arrival, and alleges to have been confronted by XXXX, who knew of her return because of his police connection.

She was taken by force again, by XXXX, and held against her will. While he was away, she was able to contact an agent, who arranged for the claimant's departure, on XXXX XXXX, 2009. She arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, and was told that since her passport was false she would be detained.

While in Canada, she has learned that XXXX, is searching for her in Guyana, and had left messages for her in Toronto, where she was staying. The claimant believes she would be at risk of domestic abuse by XXXX, her former common-law partner if she returns to Guyana. Identity and Country of Reference

I accept that the claimant is a citizen of Guyana, due to the evidence provided: A letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX,11 who says she knows XXXX XXXX, "through her sister....whom my sister had a relationship with...and still wants to kill my sister XXXX XXXX.....my family lives in Guyana." Another letter, from XXXX XXXX,12 acknowledges, that she writes for her "Aunt XXXX XXXX" and a letter from XXXX XXXX,13 who writes on behalf of "my daughter XXXX" and finally, a letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX14 who writes, "a man that have my sister XXXX aka XXXX life a miserable hell...a XXXX XXXX in Guyana." The claimant's testimony, showed familiarity with Guyana, and combined with these letters; I accept that the claimant is from that country.

The claimant arrived with a passport bearing the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX which it was admitted was fraudulently obtained15 on entry into Canada. She also had in her possession a Birth Certificate,16 indicating her name was XXXX XXXX born in Guyana on XXXX XXXX, 1962.
The claimant admitted that she had a history of criminality in the USA, to the border official, and was detained on entry.

The claim was heard on June 10, 2011, and a decision was made, excluding her on the basis of the operation of Section 98 of the IRPA and Section F(b), of Article 1 of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees ("Article 1F (b)" the claimant on July 6, 2011. The Reasons for the decision went to Judicial Review, and that decision was overturned on April 30, 2012 and returned to the Board for rehearing. This is the decision from the hearing which was heard De Novo. Summary of Findings

Having carefully considered all of the evidence before me, I find that the exclusion clause 1 F(b) is applicable to the claimant as I find that there are serious reasons for considering that the claimant has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to her admission to that country as a refugee. My reasons for this finding are set out below. Exclusion Clause Article 1F(b)
Section 98 of the IRPA17 indicates that persons to whom Article 1(E) or (F) of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees applies are not considered to be protected persons.

The relevant portion of Article 1 of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees18 states: Article 1(F). The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any person with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: (b) he has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee.
The Minister has reproduced the basis of intervention and the relevant rules, law and elements required for intervention which are referred to in the documents.19
The Minister's position is that the claimant should be excluded from protection under the Convention because of her criminal history in the USA. Whether the Crime is Serious

In Jayasekara the Federal Court of Appeal20 determined criteria for the interpretation of the exclusion clause in Article 1F(b), as regards the seriousness of a crime. It requires an evaluation of the elements of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed, the facts, and the mitigating and aggravating circumstances underlying the conviction. A presumption that a crime is serious may be rebutted by the assessment of those factors and it is important to be mindful of the hybrid nature offences in Canada and the other country and the relevance of the choice in the mode of prosecution and if there was a substantial difference between the penalty prescribed for a summary conviction offence and that for an indictable offence. Summary of the Claimant's Convictions 1. A conviction of grand larceny, in the 3rd degree, class D felony, PL 155.35, arrested XXXX XXXX XXXX 1991, convicted XXXX XXXX 1992 on a plea of guilty and sentenced to 5 years probation, which was discharged XXXX XXXX XXXX, 1997 due to her incarceration for the conviction in 1996 below;21The Canadian Criminal equivalent, is one of Offences Against rights of Property, in the section entitled Theft, 322 (1); 330 (1) Theft by a person required to account; or under Offences resembling Theft such as 342 (Theft, forgery etc. of credit card). The maximum punishment for the first two offenses, provide for a punishment for a tem not exceeding ten years at s. 334 (a) which is the same for the third 342 (1) (e). 2. A conviction of grand larceny arrested in XXXX 1995, 3rd degree, class D felony, PL 155.35, forgery, 2nd degree, Class D felony PL 170.10. In this case she was convicted in XXXX 1996, after a plea of guilty to attempted grand larceny, Class E Felony, PL 110/155.35 and sentenced to 18 month to 3 years and some restitution and after being admitted to a Correctional Facility in XXXX 1996 she was released in XXXX 1997, and paroled to US Immigration; The Canadian equivalent for this crime most closely resembles Forgery described in s. 366 (1) in that the claimant made a false document, knowing it to be false, such as the cheques of the XXXX XXXX she worked for, and with the intent that it should be used as genuine, to the prejudice of the XXXX, who was supposedly her friend. In this case, the punishment described at s. 367 involves a term of up to 14 years. 3. A conviction after being arrested XXXX XXXX XXXX 2006 for possession of a forged instrument, class D felony, PL 170.25 forgery, 2nd degree; deed, will co, Class D felony PL 170.10, falsifying business records, 1st degree, class E Felony, PL 175.10, and she was convicted XXXX XXXX XXXX 2006 on a plea of guilty to falsify business records, 1st degree, Class E felony, PL 175.10 and sentenced to a range between 18 months and 3 years and some restitution, and the claimant was admitted to the same facility as before in XXXX 2007 until XXXX 2008 and paroled to US Immigration.22 The Canadian equivalent, in this case, seems more appropriately to resemble "Personation" S. 403 as the claimant fraudulently personated a person so as to gain a job, for herself, because she knew that having a criminal record, would disqualify her from the particular job. In this case the maximum penalty is also 10 years.

It is noted that the criminal history of the claimant was determined, through an R.C.M.P. fingerprint comparison, which were found to be identical to XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX, 1962, and taken from the claimant's fingerprints, on entry to Canada XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009.
The claimant admitted that she was convicted of the crimes in the USA but claimed that there were mitigating circumstances that underlie these events which have to be considered.23

Referring to the section of the law concerned, and the jurisprudence, the panel notes that the fact that the claimant completed her sentence doesn't mean that that she cannot be excluded for the crime.24 It is also noted that the claimant need not have been charged or convicted of a crime, as the clause in question, refers to "committing" a crime. The standard of proof is "serious reasons for considering" which is less than a "balance of probabilities."25

In evaluating the seriousness of the crimes, the panel can refer to the view which Canadian law takes of that offence. The Minister has provided documentary evidence, which included the certificates of Disposition26 as well as printout details of the offences in question.27

Referring to the first (1.) offence noted above, grand larceny, which was from an arrest in 1991, and conviction in 1992, the Minister's position is that to be serious the Canadian offense would not have generated a 10 year sentence, as the amount in question was determined to be under $3000. As a result, that particular offense should not be considered "serious",

Regarding the second (2.) Offense; The claimant worked as a XXXX XXXX for an agency in Long Island New York from 1992 to 1995. She worked for XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant was supposed to be helping her. On questioning by the Minister and her counsel about the circumstances surrounding the charges the claimant admitted that she lived in the USA as XXXX XXXX, not as XXXX XXXX, and that she had to endure living with XXXX XXXX, as she was married to him, that she had to give him all her money, a way of keeping peace with him. She explains in her PIF28, that XXXX XXXX XXXX was a friend of hers and she used to give her checks, and she was asked what she did with the cheques from XXXX XXXX XXXX? She said the XXXX was involved, and that she remembered putting two cheques in the bank. She said that she did these things "to run away". She was asked if she told the judge about why she did these things, and she did not recall what the judge said.

Regarding the two other offenses, arrest in XXXX 1995, convicted in 1996, for which she served time for a year; and then the second offense which occurred 10 years later, for which she served an another year, the claimant stated that she was not thinking straight, that her self-esteem was very low, and that she "wanted to run away and kill herself." She was asked if during the court process she had the opportunity to tell the court about why she committed the crimes. She said she was speaking to a counselor, who was of no help, and that they sent her to classes. She said her mind was not clear. The panel finds that the claimant admits that she was offered assistance, but dismissed it, because of her state of mind. In reviewing the notes the panel also notes that the claimant did state that this counseling and the classes was for the previous matter, and the claimant doesn't recall what the judge said to her when she explained why she committed the crimes. The claimant had counsel, and despite her state of mind she represented by legal counsel and had an opportunity to state her case.

The Minister presented evidence that the claimant was identified by the media, as having swindled an XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX of $15,000, which was the amount of restitution was $15,000 29 and the claimant stated that XXXX XXXX XXXX was a friend, and yet she put XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXs name on blank checks to the XXXX. The claimant pled guilty to this offense, according to the court records, as she clearly had had an opportunity to state her case.

She was asked during the hearing about the lesser matter in 1992 when she worked at XXXX. In that case she said that she was "being pressured" and that she was trying to get away. She said she had "no where to turn no one I could trust, and I was thinking of my children...." She was asked what she did with the money, and her immediate response was, "I don't know." She was asked again, "don't you know what you did with it, the money?" The claimant replied, "...the credit card was mine...it wasn't cash money...people were coming and crediting back, and not thinking about it....my self esteem was low." The panel observed the claimant, and though she was candid about what she did, the added element, "my self-esteem was low" is an evaluation that the claimant has made on her own, of herself. The panel's observation, that the claimant needed money, probably did think of her children, but then proceeded to steal from the place where she was employed, anyway. She does not seem to be aware, or possibly pretended not to be present to the crime of theft. That the money was not in cash, it was a credit card, that she was being pressured by some others. This crime in itself was not serious, according to the criteria, however, the panel notes, she was XXXX XXXX, at the time, which she is now saying is not her real name, which is contrary to identity documents such as the Birth Certificate she has provided.

The claimant was asked about the third conviction (3.) in 2006, which was 10 years after the conviction for forging cheques from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The panel notes that there is no requirement, to consider a claimant's "good character" despite the passage of time, in this particular case the claimant might have been "good" for ten years, but then was arrested and convicted again while working at XXXX XXXX XXXX.30 The claimant in this case, was using another identity, XXXX XXXX, knowing she could not get a job, as XXXX XXXX, because of her criminal record.

She was asked when and why she obtained a driver's license in the name of XXXX XXXX, and she stated that she needed to drive to get to work. She was asked if she knew it was illegal to use a different name, and the claimant said yes, but that she was not thinking right, at the time. The claimant was asked questions about whether she knew it was illegal to steal money, or commit larceny, and she appeared to have drifted off. The panel drew a negative inference, from her reply that she was not thinking straight at the time. The panel found that she was aware it was illegal to use another person's identity, but she did it anyway. The panel drew a negative inference as to the fact that she would again present herself as someone else so as to work in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, despite having been charged and convicted for forging cheques of an XXXX XXXX, in the ten years before. It shows that she is intending to act falsely; she is pretending to be someone else, obtaining a driver's license in someone else's name to document her identity so that she can work again, for XXXX XXXX. The panel drew a negative inference for her attempt to conceal her identity. The panel finds that she is very resourceful, with a consistent intention to act falsely. As a result, the panel did not trust her and found her to be not credible.

She was also asked about her third conviction by her counsel and she stated that it was while she was using her cousin's identity to work in Long Island. At the time, she stated that she was trying to get away, from her ex-abuser XXXX, whom she had seen in New York at around that time, at a restaurant. This reply caused the claimant to have a strong physical reaction in the hearing room.
Overall the panel did not find the claimant credible, and the panel did not find that there were mitigating factors that would minimize the seriousness of the crimes.

The Minister has provided aggravating circumstances for the underlying convictions. For example the 1996 conviction for attempted grand larceny concerned XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, whom the claimant referred to as a friend "who used to give me cheques as gifts".31 She also adds that "The XXXX took some blank cheques from XXXX XXXX XXXX. I also signed XXXX XXXX XXXX name on some cheques and put those into my account." The claimant is admitting the crime and yet blaming another person, the XXXX. The Minister suggests that the claimant is attempting to minimize the gravity, that there was someone else involved. The Minister showed that there was news coverage of the crime in the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX,32 regarding this particular crime, showing that the claimant, then known as XXXX XXXX, was convicted of forging $15,000 in cheques drawn on the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX account. The panel notes that the claimant is very confused, and troubled. In the PIF she claims XXXX XXXX XXXX is a friend, while signing cheques with her name and depositing it to her account on behalf of the XXXX. The panel just doesn't believe the claimant about her role in this matter as being a friend to XXXX XXXX XXXX. The panel finds that the court record, the media reports, all show a consistent story, which is incongruent with the claimant's testimony.

The third conviction, in 2006, refers to an offence of falsifying business records in the USA. Which could be considered section 368 "uttering forged document" which is a hybrid offence that carries a maximum term of 10 years imprisonment if prosecuted by way of indictment or s. 403, Personation. The claimant secured employment at another XXXX XXXX, by way of assuming another person's identity, her cousin. As a result of this offense she was deported back to Guyana. The claimant was asked why she did that; she replied because she could not get a job as XXXX XXXX.

She also stated that she did not realize her true name until many years later. She was asked why she thought she could not get a job as XXXX XXXX, and she said because of her criminal past, and because my abuser XXXX was getting away with things. Did you know it was illegal to use a different name? Her reply, "yes but I wasn't thinking right." The panel feels empathy for the claimant who no doubt was trying to make a living, however, she kept going back to the past behaviors, working for XXXX whom she had stolen from, and she had stolen from XXXX, a previous employer, and continuing to work for the XXXX while pretending to be someone else. This pattern extends from 1991-2006, after serving two terms in a maximum security facility, one of which could have been in Canada, for a maximum term of 14 years. The panel finds that all these elements point to serious reasons to exclude the claimant. Non-political Crime

The crimes are non-political as the claimant wanted money. There was no political motive, no political disturbance related to any struggle to modify or abolish a government policy or a government. The claimant stated that she was running away, or trying to keep the peace with her husband so had to give him money.
As a result the crimes that the claimant was charged with in the USA are non-political crimes.

The claimant was tried in the United States of America, and was prosecuted according to rules of law that are considered democratic, and she had counsel, as she clearly responded to questions about what she told her lawyer, and the counselor, and courses she was given, that she said were not useful. The Minister provided background information on the mitigating factors of the crimes as well as the claimant.

The claimant provided documents such as a medical report,33 showing that the claimant suffered from Battered Women Syndrome, Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, and Dissociative Identity Disorder. As a result of that report it was argued that the claimant should be treated as a Vulnerable Person, and that the underlying circumstances should be considered in light of her claim for protection. This was allowed, in the original hearing, however it was not dealt with in the present hearing. The Gender guidelines34, were considered.

The claimant, provided identity documents such as a Birth Certificate, for XXXX XXXX35 which it was noted did not have seal, as well as a marriage certificate, and Divorce Certificate in Ontario, for XXXX XXXX XXXX, made here in Ontario, and dated XXXX XXXX, 2010,36 which is consistent with a Marriage Certificate also provided 37 and a copy of passport38 from Guyana, all of which identify the claimant consistently, as XXXX XXXX, and later XXXX. I do not believe that the claimant, has another identity, and I have treated the claimant as XXXX XXXX, as her fingerprints are consistent with that identity, which I accept as valid, as well as the above documents.

Notwithstanding these documents, this claimant, who arrived on a fraudulent passport, is now claiming that her real name is XXXX XXXX as she asserts her real biological mother "gave" her to XXXX XXXX many years ago. There is no valid document to support this. The panel, referred to the medical opinion39 which states: "I have not yet followed her long enough to identify discrete multiple personalities, but given her extremely traumatic history, the presence of these is not unlikely and could explain her incongruent behaviors. It could explain why she would have committed credit card theft and forging cheques without having being able to appreciate that her actions were illegal....she is having trouble problems with memory and concentration."

The medical opinion confirms what the panel observed throughout the hearing, "incongruent behaviour". What the claimant says, for example in the PIF, does not go with the facts that are revealed by the Minister's documents. The claimant attempted to minimize her involvement, and continues to act in ways that continue her history, which now extends over a 15-year period of time, such as entering Canada with a fraudulent passport, and purporting to be a different person, with a different name and birth certificate. The claimant has been convicted of theft, forgery, and personation. For the claim, she is pretending that she now really someone else, and has one birth certificate, and some personal letters as evidence, frankly, the panel is not persuaded. The panel sees a woman who has made a life of false pretenses, by words and actions; even entering Canada, with a false passport. The panel does not believe the sincerity of the pauses, the tears, the drifts during sentences, as evidence that she is suffering from anything more serious than an intent to deceive. The medical opinion, confirms what I observed. To me the inconguence, had less to do with having been battered, or abandoned, but more to do, with having an intention to represent a condition, in order to persuade that it is a fact. I am not persuaded.
The panel finds that the Minister has met the burden of showing that the claimant has committed serious non-political crimes outside Canada, prior to her admission. Burden and Standard of Proof

The Minister's counsel has the burden of proving that the claimant should be excluded from protection. The standard of proof required by the IRPA is that there be "serious reasons for considering".40 In Mugesera, the Supreme Court held that this standard requires something more than suspicion or conjecture, but something less than proof on a balance of probabilities.41
In the present case, the excludable crimes under consideration are serious non-political crimes.42

In Chan 43 the court stated that "had the appellant engaged in similar conduct in Canada, he would have been convicted of an offence such as drug trafficking for which a maximum prison term of ten years or more could have been imposed. In other words, for present purposes I will presume, without deciding, that a serious non political crime is to be equated with one in which a maximum sentence of ten years or more could have been imposed had the crime been committed in Canada."

I find that the claimant's explanations for her vagueness on the first charge in 1991, and then the second conviction in 1996, followed by the third in 2006, show a pattern of behavior of a thief, and a con-woman. I didn't believe her.

I find that there are serious reasons for considering that the claimant was convicted of crimes of a serious non-political nature and, thus, is a person referred to in Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention. Thus, the Refugee Protection Division determines that the claimant is excluded from the refugee protection afforded Convention refugees and persons in need of protection and, accordingly, rejects her claim.

The panel finds that the claimant is excluded from protection.
